title: Distributed Transactions & Data Consistency Patterns
summary: Quick revision notes on why distributed transactions fail, how sagas, the outbox pattern, CQRS and event sourcing solve it, and what eventual consistency costs you.

chapters.title: Distributed Transaction Problems
points: Mental model: one business operation spans several services, each with its own database, so no single ACID transaction can cover it
Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator sends prepare, collects votes, then sends commit or abort; it is blocking, because a coordinator crash leaves participants holding locks
The dual-write problem: updating the DB and publishing to a broker are two separate steps, so a crash between them leaves the two out of sync
CAP and partitions: during a network partition you choose consistency or availability, and most microservices choose availability
Gotcha: retries without idempotency cause duplicate side effects such as double charges, so every step needs an idempotency key

chapters.title: Saga Pattern: Choreography vs Orchestration
points: Saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes it if a later step fails
Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central controller; it is loosely coupled but the flow is hard to trace and cyclic dependencies creep in
Orchestration: a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks state; the flow is easy to follow, but the orchestrator is a coupling point to keep thin
Example: Order -> reserve stock -> charge payment -> ship; if payment fails, run release stock then cancel order, in reverse order
Gotcha: sagas are not isolated, so concurrent sagas see intermediate state; counter this with semantic locks, a pending status, or commutative updates
Gotcha: compensations must be idempotent and retryable, and they cannot undo irreversible actions such as sending an email

chapters.title: Outbox Pattern
points: Outbox: write the business row and an outbox event row in the same local DB transaction, which removes the dual-write problem
A relay publishes outbox rows to the broker, either by polling the table or by CDC (log tailing, e.g. Debezium); CDC has lower latency and no polling load
Delivery is at-least-once, because the relay can crash after publishing but before marking the row sent, so consumers must be idempotent
Inbox pattern: the consumer records processed message IDs in a table and skips duplicates, in the same transaction as its own update
Gotcha: preserve ordering per aggregate by keying messages on the aggregate ID, and purge sent outbox rows so the table does not grow forever

chapters.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing
points: CQRS: separate the write model (commands that change state) from the read model (queries over denormalized views), each scaled and stored independently
Read models are built by projections that consume events from the write side, so reads lag writes and are eventually consistent
Event sourcing: store an append-only log of immutable events as the source of truth; current state is a fold (replay) of the events for an aggregate
Snapshots: save state every N events so rebuilding an aggregate does not replay the whole stream
Event sourcing and CQRS are independent: CQRS works without event sourcing, but event sourcing almost always needs CQRS for queries
Gotcha: events are immutable, so fix mistakes with compensating events and handle schema changes by versioning or upcasting old events

chapters.title: Eventual Consistency in Practice
points: Eventual consistency: if no new updates arrive, all replicas and read models converge to the same value, but reads in between may be stale
Read-your-writes: after a write, route that user's reads to the primary or wait for the projection to reach the write's version
Idempotent consumers use a dedupe key, since at-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal
Choose the pattern: strong consistency inside one service's DB, saga across services, 2PC only for a small number of trusted XA resources
Gotcha: do not build sagas, CQRS or event sourcing for simple CRUD; each adds operational cost, so use them only where the business needs them

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Distributed Consistency Patterns
points: Problem to pattern: cross-service atomicity -> saga; DB plus broker write -> outbox; read/write scaling -> CQRS; full audit and replay -> event sourcing
Saga choice: choreography for 2-4 simple steps, orchestration for complex or branching flows
Delivery rule: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers gives effectively-once processing
Compensation rule: undo in reverse order, make it idempotent, and never rely on rollback
Checklist: idempotency key, outbox row in the same transaction, versioned events, projection lag monitoring
